taxes.base: Income of individuals and companies resident in Mexico (worldwide) and Mexican-source income of non-residents.
taxes.payer: Individuals and companies; employers withhold on wages.

rate.headline: Individuals 1.92%–35%; companies 30% flat
details: Individuals: monthly and annual tariff with 11 brackets from 1.92% to 35% (LISR art. 96 and 152).
Companies: 30% of taxable profit; small taxpayers may use RESICO (rates from 1% to 2.5% of income).
Border regions: a decree continues a 30% reduction of ISR for residents and businesses in the northern and southern border regions (renewed by decree of 31 Dec 2025).

instruments.explanation: The largest source of federal tax revenue. In the public accounts ISR appears as the 'Sistema Renta', which also includes minor legacy income-based taxes.
exceptions: Oil contractors and PEMEX are taxed under the Ley de Ingresos sobre Hidrocarburos instead.

taxes.base: Sales of goods, provision of services, temporary use of goods and imports.
taxes.payer: Consumers; businesses charge and credit it.

rate.headline: 16% general; 8% in border regions; 0% on basics and exports
details: Zero rate on basic foods, medicines and exports; exemptions include education, most medical services and housing rents.
A border-region decree halves the IVA (8%) for the northern and southern borders.

instruments.explanation: The federal consumption tax; the second-largest federal tax. VAT revenue on imports rose in 2025 with the higher peso price of imports and anti-smuggling measures.
exceptions: Small taxpayers under RESICO have simplified compliance.

names.official: Impuesto Especial sobre Producción y Servicios (IEPS) a combustibles automotrices

taxes.base: Sales of gasoline and diesel, by litre.
taxes.payer: Producers and importers; passed on at the pump.

rate.headline: Fixed quota per litre, reduced by weekly fiscal stimuli
details: Quotas per litre by fuel grade are updated each year; when pump prices rise the government applies stimuli that offset the tax, so actual collection varies week by week.

instruments.explanation: Federal fuel excise. Its yield is a policy choice as much as a tax: it absorbs price shocks. IEPS on fuels rose 5.2% in real terms in 2025 but was 6.2% below plan.
exceptions: Border regions receive additional stimuli on fuel sales (decree of 31 Dec 2025).

names.official: IEPS – tabaco, bebidas alcohólicas, bebidas azucaradas, alimentos no básicos, juegos con apuestas y otros
names.common: Excise on tobacco, alcohol, sugary drinks and gaming

taxes.base: Tobacco, alcohol, sugary and sweetened drinks, energy drinks, high-calorie foods, pesticides, gambling and (from 2026) certain video games.
taxes.payer: Producers, importers and operators; passed on to consumers.

rate.headline: Ad valorem and per-litre rates; 2026 increases on sugary drinks, tobacco and gaming
details: 2026: quota on sugary and sweetened drinks up from 1.6451 to 3.0818 pesos per litre; cigarettes ad valorem 200% (from 160%) plus a per-cigarette quota of 0.8516 pesos rising to 1.1584 by 2030.
Gaming and betting, including online, 50% (from 30%); a new tax of up to 8% on violent video games.
Alcohol: 26.5%, 30% or 53% by alcohol content.

instruments.explanation: Taxes on products the government wants to discourage. The Paquete Económico 2026 raised several of them; the yield in 2025 fell 3.5% in real terms.
exceptions: A decree gives the national lottery a fiscal stimulus of 40% of the IEPS due on betting and draws (31 Dec 2025).

instruments.statusNote: From 1 January 2026 tariffs were raised on selected tariff lines for imports from countries with which Mexico has no trade agreement.

taxes.base: Customs value of imported goods, by tariff classification and origin.

rate.headline: 0%–35% in the LIGIE; up to 50% on selected lines from non-treaty countries (2026)
details: Preferential or zero rates under Mexico's free-trade agreements (including USMCA).
Low-value parcels from non-treaty countries pay a global rate of 17% (USD 50–117) or 19% (USD 117–2,500), according to the 2025 public account.

instruments.explanation: Customs duties collected at the border. Collections rose 20% in real terms in 2025, helped by a weaker peso, stricter controls on low-value imports and the rush ahead of 2026 tariff rises.
exceptions: A basic-basket decree exempts many food imports from tariff.

taxes.base: Sale or import of new vehicles, by price.

rate.headline: Progressive tariff by vehicle price
details: Rates rise with price; lower-priced vehicles pay little or nothing.

instruments.explanation: A small federal tax on new cars. The federal vehicle-ownership tax (tenencia) was repealed in 2012; some states levy their own.
exceptions: Vehicles for public transport and hybrids/electric may be exempt or reduced.

taxes.base: Use of public assets (water, spectrum, mining concessions) and receipt of federal services (registration, migration, customs procedures).
taxes.payer: Users of the asset or service.

rate.headline: Tariffs set in the Ley Federal de Derechos by service or asset
details: Includes special mining rights on profits and rights on water extraction; rates are fixed amounts or percentages by item.

instruments.explanation: In Mexican law a 'derecho' is a contribution paid for a public service or for using public property, not a tax. Federal derechos rose 6.5% real in 2025.
exceptions: Oil-related derechos are collected through the Fondo Mexicano del Petróleo; see the oil-revenue core.

names.official: Ingresos petroleros del Gobierno Federal (transferencias del Fondo Mexicano del Petróleo)

taxes.base: Hydrocarbon production under assignments to PEMEX and contracts with private companies (profit-sharing and royalties).

rate.headline: Rates set in the Ley de Ingresos sobre Hidrocarburos and the annual budget law
details: Payments are received by the Fondo Mexicano del Petróleo and then transferred to the federal budget.

instruments.explanation: Resource income the state receives as owner of the oil, mainly from PEMEX. It is not a tax. Oil revenue was 14.7% below plan in 2025.
exceptions: PEMEX's own sales revenue is separate and not federal government revenue.

names.official: Cuotas y aportaciones de seguridad social (IMSS e ISSSTE)

taxes.base: Salaries subject to contribution (SBC) of private-sector workers (IMSS) and federal public employees (ISSSTE).
taxes.payer: Employers, workers and, in part, the federal government.

rate.headline: Several branches with employer, worker and government shares
details: IMSS covers sickness and maternity, disability and life, retirement, occupational risks and childcare; ISSSTE has its own schedule.
Employer contributions to the retirement branches rise gradually to 2030 under the 2020 pension reform.

instruments.explanation: Compulsory contributions that fund health and pensions. They are collected by the institutes, not the tax agency, and are counted in public-sector budgetary revenue but not in federal government revenue.
exceptions: INFONAVIT housing deposits (5% of wages) and AFORE retirement accounts are separate worker funds.

names.official: Impuesto sobre nóminas y asimilables (impuesto sobre erogaciones por remuneración al trabajo personal)

taxes.base: Total remuneration paid to employees in the state.

rate.headline: Varies by state – commonly 2% to 4%
details: Mexico City levies 3%; each state sets its own rate and exemptions.

instruments.explanation: The most important own-source tax of Mexican states.
exceptions: Some states exempt small employers or new jobs.

names.official: Impuestos estatales sobre tenencia o uso de vehículos

taxes.base: Ownership or use of vehicles, by value and age.

rate.headline: Varies by state – some states charge none
details: The federal tenencia was repealed in 2012; states can keep their own vehicle taxes, and several do, often only for higher-value vehicles.

instruments.explanation: An annual vehicle levy where the state chooses to charge one.

names.official: Impuestos estatales sobre hospedaje, diversiones, espectáculos y loterías

taxes.base: Hotel stays, entertainment, gambling prizes and similar services.

rate.headline: Varies by state – lodging commonly 2% to 5%
details: Mexico City taxes lodging at 3%.

instruments.explanation: Small taxes on tourism and entertainment. State taxes on similar bases must respect coordination rules on VAT.
exceptions: Not every state levies each of these taxes.

names.official: Derechos estatales (registro público, placas y refrendo, licencias, servicios)

taxes.base: State services such as vehicle plates and annual renewal, public registries, notary services and licences.

rate.headline: Varies by state and service
details: Fixed fee schedules set in each state's revenue law.

instruments.explanation: Charges for state services, often a bigger own-revenue source than many state taxes.

taxes.base: Cadastral value of land and buildings.

rate.headline: Varies by municipality – rates approved by the state congress
details: Municipalities administer the tax and keep the revenue; the state congress approves the rates in each year's municipal revenue law.

instruments.explanation: The municipal backbone tax. Low cadastral values keep its yield small compared with transfers from the federation.
exceptions: Federal property is immune; many states give discounts to the elderly or for early payment.

names.official: Impuesto sobre adquisición de bienes inmuebles (traslado de dominio)
names.native: Impuesto sobre adquisición de bienes inmuebles

taxes.base: Value of real estate transferred by sale, inheritance or similar acts.

rate.headline: Varies by municipality – commonly 2% to 4.5%
details: Set in each state's municipal revenue law.

instruments.explanation: A tax on transfers of real estate.
exceptions: Some states apply reductions for first homes.

names.official: Derechos municipales (agua potable, alumbrado público, licencias y permisos, limpia)

taxes.base: Water supply, street lighting, waste collection, licences and permits.

rate.headline: Varies by municipality and service
details: Set in municipal revenue laws approved by the state congress.

instruments.explanation: Fees for municipal services, the largest own revenue of many municipalities after the property tax.
exceptions: Street-lighting fees (DAP) have been challenged in court where set as a tax on electricity.

legalRefs.locator: art. 115 fr. III and IV inciso c
